“Oh, your father can certainly spare you if your mother can. Daughters never matter as much to a father. If you stay another full month, I can take one of you as far as London, since I am going there for a week early in June. Dawson does not mind sitting beside the driver, so there will be plenty of room for one of you. In fact, if the weather is cool, I would not object to taking both, since neither of you is large.”

“You are very kind, madam, but I think we must keep to our original plan.”

Lady Catherine seemed to accept this. “Mrs. Collins, you must send a servant with them. You know I always speak plainly. I cannot bear the thought of two young women traveling alone in hired carriages. It is extremely improper. You must find someone to accompany them. I utterly disapprove of such things. Young women should always have proper protection and attendants suited to their position. When my niece Georgiana went to Ramsgate last summer, I insisted that two male servants accompany her. Miss Darcy, the daughter of Mr. Darcy of Pemberley and Lady Anne, could not properly have traveled any other way. I pay great attention to these details. You must send John with the young ladies, Mrs. Collins. I am glad I thought to mention it. Allowing them to go alone would reflect very badly on you.”

“My uncle is sending a servant to collect us.”

“Oh, your uncle! He employs a male servant, does he? I am glad you have someone who thinks of these matters. Where will you change horses? Bromley, of course. Mention my name at the Bell, and they will look after you.”

Lady Catherine had many more questions about the journey. Since she did not answer every one herself, Elizabeth had to pay attention. She thought this fortunate: with so much on her mind, she might otherwise have forgotten where she was. She had to save her reflections for time alone. Then she welcomed them as her greatest relief. Every day she took a solitary walk, free to enjoy all the pleasure of painful memories.

She was close to knowing Mr. Darcy’s letter by heart. She studied every sentence, and her feelings toward him changed greatly from moment to moment. Remembering the way he had addressed her still filled her with anger. But when she considered how unfairly she had judged and accused him, that anger turned toward herself, and she felt compassion for his disappointed hopes.

“But when I saw someone else fall in love with you, when I imagined you loved as something other than a sacred image of beauty and goodness, or loving another more passionately than you loved me, the demon inside me woke. I sent your lover away, and from that moment I have had no peace. I searched in vain for sleep or rest. My eyes would not close, and my blood was constantly in turmoil. I entered a new life as someone dying in hope might wake in hell. I will not stain your imagination with an account of my struggles, my fury at myself, and my despair. Let a veil cover the unimaginable feelings of a guilty father. The secrets of a heart in such agony must not be exposed to common view. Everything was chaos, wrongdoing, remorse, and hatred, yet still the tenderest love. The sight of your bitter, sympathetic grief first made me firmly resolve to overcome my passion and restore a father to my child. That brought me here. I thought that if I could revive my grief for your mother and the memories of her that had slept for seventeen years, all love for her daughter would die. In a burst of courage I decided to come alone, to leave you, the life within my life, and not see you again until I could do so without guilt. But it was impossible. I had overestimated my strength or underestimated my love. I would certainly have died if you had not hurried to me. If only my life had indeed ended!

“And now, Mathilda, I must make my final confession. I was terribly mistaken in believing I could conquer my love for you. I never can. Seeing this house, these fields and woods where my first love lived seems only to have strengthened it. In my madness I dared tell myself: Diana died to bring her into the world; her mother’s spirit passed into her body, and she should be Diana to me. Every attempt to cast off this love makes it cling more tightly. This guilty love, more unnatural than hatred, destroys your hopes and ruins me forever.

“It would have been better to love despair, and safer to kiss her.

“No passage of time or distance can tear from my soul what has become part of it. Since coming here, I have not escaped for one moment the hell of passion planted within me, burning until everything is cold, rigid, and dead.

His story was that, on his journey from home through Datchet, smoke rising from the inn’s chimney had surprised him. Supposing he might find fellow travellers gathered within, he knocked and was received. The house contained only Lucy and her mother. An attack of rheumatism had deprived the latter of the use of her limbs, and the country’s remaining inhabitants had departed one after another, leaving them behind. Lucy implored him to remain; in a week or two her mother would improve, and they could then begin their journey. Left so helpless and deserted, they must perish. He replied that his wife and children were already with the emigrants and that, in his judgment, staying was therefore impossible. As her final resource, Lucy entrusted him with a letter for Idris, to be handed to her wherever he encountered us. This duty, at least, he performed, and Idris received with deep feeling the letter that follows:

“Honoured Lady,

“I am certain you will remember and compassionate me, and I venture to hope for your assistance; what other hope remains? Forgive this confused way of writing; I scarcely know what I do. A month since, my dear mother lost the use of her limbs. Already she has improved, and in another month I am sure she could travel by the means you so kindly offered to provide. But everyone has left us now—everyone. Each person, when departing, said perhaps my mother would recover before we were altogether abandoned. Three days ago I called on Samuel Woods, who, because of his newborn child, had stayed until the end. They were a numerous family, and I hoped to persuade them to wait a little longer on our account; instead, I found their home empty. Since then I have seen no living soul until this kind man came. What is to become of us? My mother knows nothing of our position. Her illness is so severe that I have concealed it from her.

“Will you not send somebody to our aid? In our present state we must, I am sure, die miserably. Were I to move my mother now, she would perish on the journey. And when she recovers, even if I could—I cannot imagine by what means—discover the right roads and travel those many, many miles to the coast, you would all have reached France. Between us would lie the great sea, terrible even to those who sail upon it.
